Whether a Formal Order is Indispensable Before Invoking Section 299 CrPC: A Conflict in Supreme Court Jurisprudence


There is an apparent conflict between two judgments pronounced by the Supreme Court in July 2026. In State of West Bengal v. Kader Khan Criminal Appeal Nos. 1164–1166 of 2026 (2nd Image), the Supreme Court held that it is not necessary for the trial court to pass a formal order before invoking Section 299 CrPC, i.e., recording evidence in the absence of the accused. However, in paragraph 14, the Court held that the twin conditions prescribed under Section 299(1), namely, that the accused has absconded and that there is no immediate prospect of his arrest, must exist on the date of recording of evidence. Once these conditions are satisfied, the Court held that a formal order is not necessary.

On the contrary, in Mahendra Singh v. State of Chhattisgarh Criminal Appeal No. 3566 of 2026 (1st Image), the Supreme Court expressly held in paragraph 13 that the trial court must pass a formal order recording its satisfaction that the conditions under Section 299(1) stand fulfilled before invoking the provision. In Jayendra Vishnu (Relied in Mahendra Singh ) , the Supreme Court had held that, in view of Section 3 of the Evidence Act, the jurisdictional facts contemplated under Section 299(1) must be proved by evidence led by the prosecution, and the court must record its finding regarding the existence of those jurisdictional facts before assuming jurisdiction under Section 299. Thus, the ratio in Jayendra Vishnu necessarily requires the trial court to pass a formal order after evaluating the evidence on record.

The judgment in Kader Khan failed to consider the law laid down in Jayendra Vishnu, despite the same having been expressly relied upon by the Supreme Court in Mahendra Singh. This omission assumes significance because, if the jurisdictional facts must be established by evidence and judicially determined, the recording of a formal order is an indispensable safeguard against arbitrary invocation of Section 299. It may, therefore, be argued that the view taken in Kader Khan is susceptible to being regarded as per incuriam.
